764.title: The plague of Cyprian
764.hook: when plague came, letters from two bishops describe Christians staying to nurse the sick, their own and others
764.howItsDone: Christians count visiting the sick among the works of love in Matthew 25, and some churches organize hospital visits, meals and prayers for people who are ill.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Origen reading, and your line was read deeper. Which part of the week did you read again, slower? Day seven hundred sixty-four.

"I was sick, and ye visited me." That's Jesus in Matthew's Gospel, describing the day the nations are gathered and sorted. The people who visited the sick are startled. When did we see you sick? And the answer: when you did it for the least of these, you did it for me. It's an easy line to admire on a calm day. It's a different line in a city where a disease is spreading, nobody knows how, and the sick are dying in their houses and in the streets. Two bishops, Cyprian in Carthage and Dionysius in Alexandria, lived through days like that. Their words survive. Today's word carries Cyprian's name.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Start with Dionysius. In a letter the historian Eusebius preserved, he describes what the Christians of Alexandria did during the plague, or most of them, he says. In paraphrase: out of great love, they didn't spare themselves. They clung to one another. They visited the sick without fear and cared for them, and some who nursed others caught the disease and died, taking the sickness of their neighbors on themselves. He contrasts this with others in the city who, he says, pushed the sick away and fled, even from those dearest to them. That's one bishop's account of his own people, and he's proud of them. But the picture is specific: hands that wash and feed, and a cost that's paid. In Carthage, Cyprian's deacon Pontius wrote his bishop's life. When the plague came, he says, Cyprian gathered his people and taught them that it isn't remarkable to care only for your own. If you want to be children of the Father, he told them, do good to everyone, even to those who persecute you. Then he set them to work, each by what they had: the rich gave money, the poor gave their labor. Cyprian also wrote a short book, On Mortality, for frightened Christians who were dying too, and asking why. He doesn't pretend the plague spares them. Instead he says it shows what's in people: whether the healthy care for the sick, whether families truly love each other, whether doctors stay with their patients. The heart of today isn't a statistic, and it isn't a claim that only Christians were brave. It's writing from two cities, saying the same plain thing about their people. They stayed.
screen: `THE RICH GAVE MONEY, THE POOR LABOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring someone ill to mind. Settle, and breathe. Who do you know who's sick right now? In a hospital, in bed at home, worn down by something long and quiet that others have stopped asking about. Let one face come. Think about what would actually help them this week. Not a grand gesture. A message, soup, a ride, a visit, an hour of sitting with them. Cyprian's rule fits here: give what you have, money or time or hands. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Cyprian. The bishop of Carthage in whose days a plague struck, when writers in two cities said Christians nursed the sick, their own and others, even at the cost of their lives.
Your line: they stayed. Today, check on the person you named. Call, text, knock, or bring something. Day seven hundred sixty-four.

765.title: Antony goes into the desert
765.hook: a young Egyptian hears 'go and sell that thou hast' read in church, and does it, and in time walks into the desert
765.howItsDone: Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Antony as a father of monasticism and keep his feast; monks and nuns take vows of poverty, while other Christians practice the same verse through giving and simple living.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cyprian, and your line was they stayed. Did you check on the person you named? Day seven hundred sixty-five.

A young man in an Egyptian village has just buried his parents. He's inherited good farmland, and he's responsible for his little sister. One day, on his way to church, he's turning something over in his mind: the apostles left everything to follow Jesus, and in the book of Acts, believers sold their land and laid the money at the apostles' feet. What would that even look like now? He walks in. And at that moment, the Gospel being read aloud is the one about a rich young man. His name is Antony. The story comes from his Life, written by Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria.

Here's the verse he heard, from Matthew, in the King James Bible: "If thou wilt be perfect, go and sell that thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come and follow me." Athanasius says Antony felt as if the words had been read for him. In the Gospel, the rich young man hears that and goes away sorrowful. Antony goes out of the church and does it. He gives his family's land to the people of his village. He sells the rest of what he owns and gives the money to the poor, keeping a little back for his sister. Then he walks into church again, and hears another line: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow." So he gives away what he'd kept, places his sister with a community of faithful women, and begins a life of prayer and work. And here's the honest part: he doesn't vanish into the sand that afternoon. He starts at the edge of his village, learning from an old man who lives that way. He moves out to the tombs. Only later does he cross into the desert, farther and farther in. Athanasius says he wrote the Life because monks in other places asked him what Antony was like. Christians hear this story differently. Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Antony as a father of monastic life, and in those churches the call to sell everything is a real vocation some are given. Other Christians, among them some Protestants, read the verse as aimed at what holds a person's heart, and practice it through generosity rather than leaving home. Both readings take the verse seriously. What lands in Antony's story is the speed. He heard. And he went.
screen: `THE VILLAGE EDGE, THE TOMBS, THE DESERT.`
`A VOCATION, OR A MATTER OF THE HEART?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let go of one thing. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind walk through where you live: a closet, a shelf, a drawer, a garage. Look for one thing you own that you don't need, and that someone else could use. A coat. A tool. Books. A pair of shoes. Don't pick the easiest junk. Pick something with a little weight to it. Then decide where it goes: a neighbor, a shelter, a charity shop, someone you know. If you pray, you can offer it to God as you let it go. If you don't, just hold it in your mind and open your hand. The bell holds the time.
Antony. A young Egyptian who heard go and sell that thou hast, gave it away, and step by step walked into a life of prayer in the desert.
Your line: he heard, and went. Today, give away the thing you chose, before the day is out, without waiting to feel ready. Day seven hundred sixty-five.

766.title: Constantine
766.hook: an emperor sees a sign before battle, and everything changes for the church, for good and ill
766.howItsDone: The Orthodox Church honors Constantine as a saint, together with his mother Helena; other Christians remember him as a pivotal and debated figure in the church's history with the state.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Antony, and your line was he heard, and went. What did you give away? Day seven hundred sixty-six.

For days now, the people in this story have been on the wrong side of power. A letter explaining Christians to outsiders. Justin writing to the emperor. Perpetua in the arena. Tertullian daring the governors. Cyprian's people nursing the sick in a frightened city. Today the camera turns around. A Roman ruler named Constantine is marching on Rome to fight a rival for the empire. And before the battle, by his own account, he sees something in the sky. He is not a Christian. He is about to become a very powerful friend to the church, and that changes the story.

We have two old accounts, and they don't match exactly. Eusebius, a bishop who knew Constantine, writes that the emperor himself told him, and swore to it, that around noon he saw a cross of light above the sun, with words: by this, conquer. That night, Eusebius says, Christ appeared to him in a dream and told him to make a copy of the sign and carry it into battle. So Constantine had a standard made with the first two Greek letters of Christ's name. Another writer of the time, Lactantius, tells it more simply: in a dream, Constantine was told to mark the heavenly sign of God on his soldiers' shields, and he did. A vision in the sky, or a dream, or both. The sources differ, and that's worth saying plainly. What happened next is that Constantine won, and he favored the church. Christians who had been hunted now found their emperor on their side. Their buildings could rise in public. Their bishops could meet openly. And there's the other side. When the emperor is your friend, the emperor has opinions about your church. Faith and power start to tangle in ways Christians have argued about since. Jesus had said, "My kingdom is not of this world." Now a kingdom of this world was carrying his sign into battle. Christians still weigh this differently. Some see Constantine as God's answer to the prayers of the persecuted, and the Orthodox Church honors him as a saint. Others see the moment the church began to trade the arena for the palace, and wonder what that cost. Some hold both at once. Eusebius adds one more detail. Constantine was baptized only near the end of his life.
screen: `MY KINGDOM IS NOT OF THIS WORLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think about faith and power. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place where you hold a little power: at work, at home, in a group, over someone younger or newer than you. Then ask two quiet questions. What does what I believe, about God or about people, ask of me there? And where might the power be shaping the belief, instead of the other way around? Don't rush to an answer. If you pray, you can bring that place before God. If you don't, simply look at it honestly for this minute. The bell holds the time.
Constantine. The emperor who said he saw a sign before battle, and who turned the church from hunted to favored, for good and ill.
Your line: power changes things. Today, in the place you named, use your bit of power once on behalf of someone with less. Day seven hundred sixty-six.

767.title: The Edict of Milan (313)
767.hook: Christianity becomes legal, and the persecuted become the favored
767.howItsDone: Some churches pray in their services for those in authority and for people who suffer for their faith, and some Christian groups work for religious freedom for people of every faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantine, and your line was power changes things. Where did you use your bit of power for someone with less? Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

A notice goes up on a public wall in Nicomedia, a great city of the eastern empire. It's a letter from two emperors, Constantine, who ruled the west, and Licinius, who was taking hold of the east, who have met at Milan and agreed on how the empire will treat religion. The writer Lactantius copied it out in full. And he notes where it was posted: in the same city where, by his account, an order to tear down churches and burn scriptures had been nailed up some years before. Same city, same kind of wall, opposite message. People who had hidden their books, buried their friends and kept their heads down could walk past and read it. Today's word is that letter.
screen: `A NOTICE ON A WALL IN NICOMEDIA.`

segments.voice: Here's what it actually says, in paraphrase. The emperors grant to Christians, and to all others, the free power to follow whatever religion each person chooses. Hear that again: not Christians instead of everyone else. Christians and everyone else. The letter gives a reason that sounds very Roman: so that whatever divine power there is in heaven may be kindly toward us and toward all who live under our rule. Then it gets practical. The meeting places and property taken from Christians are to be handed back, at once, without payment. And if someone had bought one of those buildings in good faith, they can ask the state for compensation. That's the part that makes it real. Freedom isn't only a sentence; it's a key returned to a door. Now the name. What we call the Edict of Milan reaches us as a letter, and Lactantius gives the copy that Licinius had posted in Nicomedia. The name stuck anyway. Then the turn: the persecuted become the favored. Eusebius keeps letters from the months that follow in which Constantine sends money to clergy in Africa and frees clergy from public duties. That goes past the wall notice. Tomorrow, an emperor calls bishops together. The first letter to Timothy had already asked prayers "for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life." Here was that quiet life, arriving all at once. And one more thing, for good and ill. The letter's words were freedom for all. Some readers point out that later, when Christians held power, that promise didn't always hold for others. The long story has both. Today, sit with the line as written.
screen: `AN EDICT THAT REACHES US AS A LETTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and breathe slowly. The letter's phrase was Christians and all others. Bring to mind one person near you whose faith is different from yours, or who has none: a neighbor, a coworker, someone in your family. Picture them on an ordinary day, keeping what they keep. A prayer, a fast, a holiday, a quiet Sunday morning with no church in it. Don't argue with it in your head. Just let them be free in the picture. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, the way that old letter named Christians and all others in one breath. If you don't pray, simply wish them well, as they are. The bell holds the time.
Constantine. One of the two emperors whose agreement at Milan gave Christians, and all others, freedom to follow their own religion, and handed back what had been taken.

Your line: freedom for all. Today, make room once for someone else's faith, or lack of one: a greeting on their holiday, or a question asked because you really want the answer. Day seven hundred sixty-seven.

768.title: Nicaea (325)
768.hook: bishops gather over Arius' teaching and write: of one substance with the Father
768.howItsDone: Christians in Orthodox, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and other churches say the Nicene Creed together in worship, standing, often on Sundays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Constantine, and your line was freedom for all. Whose different faith did you make room for? Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

One word, and it's Greek: homoousios. It's a mouthful, and yet bishops traveled across the empire to argue over it, emperors took sides, and people were sent into exile for saying it or for refusing to. Here's why. In Alexandria, a priest named Arius was teaching that the Son of God was the first and greatest thing God made. Glorious, above everything else, but made. Not God in the same way the Father is God. His bishop objected. The argument spread, the way arguments do, and the emperor Constantine called bishops together at a city called Nicaea to settle it. Today: the word they chose.

Arius wasn't a careless thinker. He was protecting something: God is one, and nothing can share God's being. So the Son, he reasoned, must be something God made. The creed that came out of Nicaea ended by rejecting a saying of his side, that there was a time when the Son was not. The bishops searched the Bible for words to answer him, Athanasius later wrote, and kept finding that Arius could agree with them. The Son is from God? Yes, he'd say, so is everything. So they reached for a word that isn't in the Bible at all. Homoousios. Of the same being. Of one substance. The Son isn't like the Father in a high and noble way. He is what the Father is. That's the move: a word from outside scripture, chosen to protect what they believed scripture was already saying. John's Gospel opens, "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." And Jesus says in John, "I and my Father are one." The bishops heard those lines as more than closeness. The creed later prayed in churches is a fuller form, which we'll meet later on this path. In the old English of the Book of Common Prayer, its lines on the Son run: "Very God of very God, Begotten, not made, Being of one substance with the Father." Very, in that old English, means true. True God from true God. Begotten, not made: a son, not a product. Why does any of this matter on an ordinary day? Because Christians who say this creed are saying that when they look at Jesus, they aren't looking at God's best creation. They're looking at God.
screen: `ARIUS: THERE WAS WHEN HE WAS NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. If the Nicene Creed is part of your tradition, you can say it now, slowly, from memory or from a page, and stop on the lines about the Son. If it isn't, take just four phrases and let them go by, one per breath. God of God. Light of light. Very God of very God. Begotten, not made. Don't try to solve them. Just notice which one catches. People argued over these words for a long time; you only have to hear them once, slowly. Then let the words go and keep breathing. The bell holds the time.
Homoousios. Greek for of the same being, of one substance. The word the bishops at Nicaea chose to say the Son is what the Father is, not something the Father made.
Your line: true god from true god. Today, notice one word you use without thinking that's actually doing a lot of work, and ask what it's protecting. Day seven hundred sixty-eight.

769.title: Athanasius against the world
769.hook: exiled again and again, he held to Nicaea when it was unpopular
769.howItsDone: Orthodox, Catholic and other churches honor Athanasius as a saint and teacher of the faith, and his On the Incarnation is still read in churches and classrooms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, homoousios, and your line was true god from true god. What everyday word did you catch doing a lot of work? Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

Winning the vote isn't the end of an argument. Nicaea chose its word, and then the argument kept going. Bishops who'd signed changed their minds. Emperors came and went, and some of them leaned toward Arius' side. And one stubborn bishop of Alexandria, named Athanasius, would not let the word go. He was sent away from his city, and came back, and was sent away again, and came back again. He hid. He wrote. He was accused of crimes, and answered the charges in writing. Later generations gave him a short Latin nickname: Athanasius contra mundum. Athanasius against the world. It didn't look like a hero on a hill. It looked like a man packing a bag, again.

What was he holding on to? In his book On the Incarnation, Athanasius gives the reason Nicaea mattered to him, in one swing of a sentence. In paraphrase: God became human, so that humans might become divine. Only God can bring people home to God, he argued. If the Son is a creature, however grand, the bridge doesn't reach. So for him homoousios wasn't a word game. It was the whole rescue. Now the exiles. He's sent as far as Trier, in Gaul, a long way from the Nile. Other times he simply disappears into Egypt, and he's sheltered, the stories say, by the desert monks. That's a thread from a few days ago: Athanasius later wrote the Life of Antony, the man who heard a Gospel line read in church, and went into the desert. Here's a surprise. When enemies mocked him for running instead of staying to die, he wrote a defense of his flight. Jesus himself withdrew when they sought to kill him, he pointed out. And Paul, in his own words, escaped Damascus this way: "through a window in a basket was I let down by the wall, and escaped his hands." Standing firm, for Athanasius, didn't mean standing still for the soldiers. It meant not changing the word. Run if you must, hide if you must, but don't sign what you believe is false. Was he easy to deal with? His opponents certainly didn't think so, and they brought real charges against him, which he denied. He could be a hard man to cross. But the nickname stuck because, for long stretches, he seemed to be nearly alone, and he didn't move.
screen: `GOD BECAME HUMAN, SO HUMANS MIGHT RISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you hold to be true that, in some room you're in, isn't popular. At work, at a family table, with friends. It doesn't need to be about faith. Let it come. Then test it, slowly. Is this a truth, or is it my pride wearing a truth's clothes? If it holds up, what's one way to hold it that isn't cruel to the people who disagree? Athanasius ran, hid and wrote. He didn't have to win every room. If you pray, you can bring this to God. If not, just sit with it. The bell holds the time.
Athanasius. The bishop of Alexandria who, exiled again and again, kept holding to the word of Nicaea when it was unpopular.
Your line: against the world. Today, if the truth you named comes up, say it once, plainly and kindly, and then let it stand. Day seven hundred sixty-nine.

770.title: Nicholas of Myra
770.hook: a bishop who, the story goes, dropped gold through a poor family's window by night
770.howItsDone: Orthodox and Catholic Christians keep a feast of Saint Nicholas, and in some countries children find small gifts in their shoes or stockings that morning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Athanasius, and your line was against the world. Did the truth you named come up, and did you say it kindly? Day seven hundred seventy.

A bag lands on the floor in the dark. It came through the window. Inside, there's gold. That's the scene at the heart of today's story, and it's an old one. A bishop named Nicholas, in Myra, a town near the southern coast of what's now Turkey. The red coat, the sleigh and the reindeer come much later, and from somewhere else entirely. Before any of that, there's a family in trouble, a window, and a man who very much didn't want to be thanked. We know little about Nicholas from records of his own time. What we have is mostly the story people told about him, again and again, and the way his church remembered him.

Here's how the old Lives of Nicholas tell it. A man in Nicholas's town had been well off and lost everything. He had three daughters, and no money for their dowries, which meant no marriages. The story says he was close to a terrible choice: letting his daughters be sold into shame to keep the household alive. Nicholas heard. He didn't knock on the door. He didn't call a meeting or make a speech. At night, he went to the house and threw a bag of gold in through the window, and left. The father woke up, found it, and wept, and the first daughter was married. Nicholas came back, another night, and did it again. And on the third night, the father was waiting. He ran after the shadow in the street, caught up, and fell at his feet. And what does Nicholas do? He begs the man to tell no one. That's the center of the story. Not the gold, the secret. It sounds like a page out of Jesus' teaching in Matthew's Gospel: "when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret." As the story tells it, Nicholas didn't want the father to owe him, or to feel watched, or to have to be grateful in public. He wanted three young women to be safe and a father to keep his dignity. Orthodox and Catholic Christians honor him as a saint, and in some places children still find gifts on his feast. Whatever the history behind it, the shape the story keeps is this: help that arrives in the dark, with no name on it.

Here's the practice: settle, and breathe. Think of someone who could use help and wouldn't like to ask for it. A neighbor, a coworker, a student, a relative quietly having a hard month. Let one person come. Now think of one gift you could give them without your name on it. Groceries left on a step. A bill paid. A gift card in an unmarked envelope. A good word about them said to someone else, when they're not there. Pick one, small enough to actually do. Then picture yourself walking away before anyone sees. If you pray, you can pray for them. The bell holds the time.
Nicholas. A bishop near the southern coast of what's now Turkey who, the story goes, threw gold through a poor family's window by night, and begged not to be thanked.
